headline: Rocky Point on the ebb: blues chew bunker, scup stack the ledges, fluke slide up the bay
subhead: The bunker schools are thick from Conimicut to Prudence and the blues found them — the harder question this week is where the bass are hiding in the heat.
body_markdown:
Stood on the Fields Point pier Thursday night watching three guys work bunker snags off the seawall, and every one of them had the same complaint — too much bait, not enough room to swing a rod. That's the story of the bay right now. Pogies are stacked from the Providence River clear down past Nyatt Point, and where you find them thick, the blues are on them like they've got a grudge. I watched a school get worked over off Rocky Point Wednesday evening, birds diving, water boiling white for maybe ninety seconds, then it moved off toward Prudence and went quiet again. That's the pattern — find the bait, get there fast, because it doesn't sit still.

We flagged this a week back — said the bluefish are a bait-driven fishery, plain and simple, and wherever the bunker re-form after a blow, the blues show up within hours. That's exactly what's playing out. No mystery to it. Snag a bunker on a treble weighted rig off the Conimicut breakwater or drift a chunk under a float off Nyatt, and if there's bait around, you're in business. Topwater poppers work when they're actively busting — a big pencil popper or a Hogy walking bait thrown right into the froth off Rocky Point has been drawing violent strikes, mostly bluefish in the 3-6 pound class with the occasional bigger one mixed in.

Bass are trickier, and I won't pretend otherwise. Surface water's sitting in the low-to-mid 70s through the bay, warm enough that the stripers are doing what they do this time of year — holding deep on structure through the daylight hours and only really committing to feed at first light, last light, and after dark. Daytime, guys jigging bucktails over the drop-offs at Conimicut Point and along the edge of the Providence River channel are picking at fish, but it's slow, technical work — bounce a half-ounce white bucktail with a curly tail trailer right on bottom in 20 to 25 feet, and you might get two or three bites in an hour where you'd have gotten ten a month ago. The real bass are coming after dark, eels and big swim shads worked slow around the bridge pilings and the rip lines off Nyatt and Rocky Point on the last two hours of the outgoing.

Here's the piece worth paying attention to heading into this weekend — the tide range is narrowing fast into the neap around August 5th and 6th. That current's going to go soft in a lot of spots that depend on hard water movement to load bait against structure. We called this one too — said last week that as the tides soften, the bass compress into the strongest current hours and the deepest, coolest structure, and that's precisely what I'd expect through the weekend. When the flow's weak, don't waste your time on the flats — go to the bridges and the channel edges where whatever current there is still concentrates. Slow your presentation down to match it. A bucktail that worked on a strong moon tide two weeks back needs to be fished twice as slow right now, or you're just pulling it past fish that can't be bothered to chase.

Fluke are the bright spot, and they're doing what fluke do in August — pushing up into the bay behind the bait. Greenwich Bay has been holding fish along the channel edges in 15 to 20 feet, and the Providence River itself has produced some surprising keepers off the deeper holes near the bridges. White Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, three-quarter ounce, dragged slow on the drift with the outgoing water — that's been the ticket. Nothing giant, mostly fish in the 18 to 20 inch range with a few better ones mixed in, but it's a dependable bite when the bass and blues are making you work for it.

Scup are exactly where you'd expect them — thick on the rocky ledges from Rocky Point down through Conimicut and out around the edges of Prudence. Sea worms or squid strips on a high-low rig, small hooks, and you can fill a bucket in an hour on the right tide stage — I like the last of the incoming through the top of the tide when the current's still moving bait past the rocks but hasn't gone full send yet. Black sea bass are mixed in on the same structure around Prudence, though the bigger ones want you fishing tight to the rock piles rather than the open sand.

Weakfish have been scarce — I haven't heard a solid report on one all month, and I'm not going to pretend they're around when they're not.

Looking ahead, I don't see a big thermal shift coming — the pattern's been stable and I'd expect it to hold through the coming week, warm water, thick bait, bass playing hard to get in daylight. If I had one evening to fish, I'd be at Rocky Point right on the tide change into dark, throwing bucktails first, then switching to eels once the light's gone. That's where the current still does something even on a softening tide, and that's where the bass are going to be.
